A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scaling RL to Long Videos and the LongVILA-R1/MR-SP framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training-stage and frame-count ablations, training-efficiency measurements, and qualitative model comparisons.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark evaluations and retained ablations and efficiency measurements, plus newly presented training-reward curves.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the stated data-selection procedure: v1 assigns easy/hard questions to CoT-SFT and medium questions to RL, whereas v4 says to discard easy/hard questions and train on the remainder. The core CoT-SFT/GRPO pipeline, objectives, embedding reuse, and MR-SP rollout/prefilling procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 removes EgoSchema, EventBench, and MVBench evaluations from Table 1, retaining six external benchmarks. Training coverage expands through 2K additional 4K-resolution videos covering settings including autonomous driving and household robotics. Section 3.2 also reports an approximately equal mixture of multiple-choice and open-ended QA, beyond v1's described multiple-choice generation pipeline.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Apollo-7B, LLaVA-Video-7B, NVILA-8B-Video, and VITA-1.5-7B, while removing VideoLLaMA2-7B from that comparison despite retaining it in Table 1. Table 1 replaces GPT-4V with GPT-4o mini. Table 2 removes GPT-4o and adds the direct LongVILA-7B backbone comparison.

E3.justification: Sections 3–4 change the training allocation substantially: CoT-SFT grows from 18K to 36K examples, the proposed RL subset from 33K to 68K, and auxiliary data decreases from 110K to 102K. The stated difficulty-filtering/allocation rule also changes. These are reported changes to training-data preparation and experimental settings; they do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 Figure 8 adds training-dynamics evidence showing overall, format, and accuracy rewards increasing and stabilizing. The frame-scaling analysis, stage/dataset ablation, efficiency comparison, and seven appendix case studies are retained. Converting v1 Figure 8 into v4 Table 4 redisplays the same frame-scaling results rather than adding an ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten timing warm-up iterations followed by averaging five iterations. Neither supplies defined seed counts, accuracy error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4's checklist asserts statistical support but provides no corresponding new statistical procedure or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 replace many scores and add/remove result entries. VideoMME accuracy changes from 62.4/68.4 to 65.1/71.1 without/with subtitles. In Table 2, LongVILA-R1's overall score changes from 67.9 to 72.0, while spatial accuracy changes from 70.0 to 53.3, below Video-R1's revised 58.5. Training data changes and unexplained benchmark rescoring prevent treating these as controlled same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The clipped GRPO objective and group-normalized advantage in Equations 1–2 are mathematically unchanged. Neither version adds formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or further theoretical derivations.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—LongVideo-Reason, two-stage reasoning training, and MR-SP—remain intact, as does the 2.1-times speedup claim. v4 adds explicit support claims for 8,192 frames and configurable FPS and updates headline dataset and performance figures. This extends the capability claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v1's limitations discuss the uncertain definition of reasoning and learning from ultra-dense video. v4 replaces this with resource constraints for longer sequences, additional modalities, and larger batches. Section 8 adds a substantive argument that caption-derived, non-identity-focused supervision reduces privacy and profiling risks. The appendix's case-study interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 identifies DeepSeek-R1-671B as the reasoning annotator, names VILA-HD for bounding-box generation, specifies 512-frame VideoMME evaluation, and adds a direct model-checkpoint link. Bounding-box reasoning already appears in v1 Figure 9, so the added attribution is documentation rather than proof of a new component. Reported annotation cost changes from 40,000 to 80,000 H100 GPU-hours.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Apollo, VITA-1.5, Qwen2-VL, and VideoLLaMA 3, and removes citations associated with omitted benchmarks and several retained baselines. Section 2 largely preserves the same positioning relative to short-video reasoning, sequence parallelism, and RL frameworks.

P1.justification: Most methodological prose, related work, and case-study explanations are retained. v4 revises the abstract and conclusion, moves limitations and broader impacts into the main paper, places the qualitative appendix after the references and new NeurIPS checklist, and makes localized wording changes. The main scientific narrative remains substantially the same.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the branded, predominantly two-column main paper with a single-column conference layout. It relocates and rearranges the efficiency plots, restructures benchmark tables, converts the frame-scaling plot into a table, adds reward plots, and resizes/repositions appendix figures. These are extensive visual changes, although many underlying figures and results are retained.

improvement.justification: v4 adds stronger comparators and a direct 7B backbone control, clarifies annotation models and access, and fixes the VideoMME prose/table mismatch. However, it removes three benchmark evaluations and leaves Table 2's rescoring and aggregation unexplained: the reported 72.0 overall differs from the 69.4 unweighted category mean despite the retained balanced-benchmark description. Unsupported statistical-reporting assertions add another concern. These benefits and shortcomings prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
